**Where to see a Kordofan giraffe in the Democratic Republic of the Congo** | Spot | What you’ll find | Why it matters | Practical notes | |------|-----------------|----------------|-----------------| | **Garamba National Park** (Haut‑Uélé Province, northeast DRC) | *Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum* – the last Kordofan giraffe population in the country (≈ 90‑100 individuals, 2024 census) | UNESCO World Heritage Site (#136, inscribed 1980); the park’s management team (African Parks & ICCN) has turned the area into a secure “conservation refuge” for the subspecies after years of poaching and civil unrest.
• The habitat (open savanna with scattered trees) lets giraffes glide through clear, open spaces—great for spotting them against a blue or orange sky. | • **Timing** – June falls in the early wet season (April‑June). Roads from the airstrip (Nagero) may be soft‑muddy; most visitors prefer the dry season (Dec‑Mar) but many still go in June. Expect fewer calves and more vegetation‑shrouded animals; sighting rates dip slightly compared with the dry season.
• **Security** – DRC’s safety rating is “High.” Always travel with the park’s armed‑ranger escort; arrangements must be made months ahead through **African Parks**.
• **Access** – Reach Nagero airstrip by private charter (or through African Parks) from Bilinga or Goma. From there the park is 50‑70 km east; field and wildlife camps are very basic (tent or walk‑in huts). | | **Zakouma National Park** (Chad – neighbour of DRC) | Same subspecies (≈ 70% of Chad’s Kordofan giraffe population). | • If you’re willing to split your trip between DRC and Chad it offers a second chance to see a Kordofan giraffe in a more dispersed environment (southern Chad, southeast district).
• The park is a “List in Danger” site (Giraffe Conservation Foundation). | • Access in Chad is easier in the dry season (Nov‑Mar); June falls inside the long rains when roads can be heavily muddied.
• Security in northern Chad is relatively stable but still recommend checking the latest travel advisory. | --- ## How to make the most of a June visit to Garamba 1. **Book early with African Parks** - They coordinate transport, permits, security, and the ranger‑guided safari or bush‑walk that is required in the park. - Provide them with your itinerary, flight schedule, and expected arrival time so they can secure an escort and location guides. 2. **Choose the right mode of transport** - **In‑park air options**: Small light aircraft can fly you to/from Nagero airstrip. Compared with travel by road, it bypasses the difficult over‑land route which is often blocked by rain. - **Ground vehicles**: 4×4 safari vehicles (usually OPV & Toyota Land Cruiser derivatives) are the standard; they’re familiar with the sandy tracks and can handle tiny lumps of loam. 3. **Pack for the wet season** - Waterproof hiking boots, a good rain jacket, a breathable hooded top, and sun‑block (the sun can still be intense). - Bring a large water bottle and repack the saliva avoid leaving waste: the park’s camps have no running water and rely on rationed supply. 4. **Plan a realistic itinerary** - **Day 1–2**: Arrival at Nagero; orientation, gear check, night safe‑watch (peaceful vie of lions & hyenas). - **Day 3–4**: “Giraffe Circuit” – guided bush‑drive and a short walk to the north‑south transect where giraffes are most often seen. - **Day 5**: Optional river‑crossing walk to spot hippos, and a sunset session on the Garamba river. - **Day 6**: Departure (or extra buffer day if roads are heavily flooded). 5. **Safety and health** - Mosquito‑netting and prophylaxis for malaria (Jun‑Oct is peak). - Health check‑up for rabies and typhoid before departing; Garamba holds ~95% of the East African Kordofan giraffes. | Each individual is a genetic reservoir; seeing them in situ underscores the need for conservation. | | **Scenic habits** | They browse in open grassland and short‑tree savanna while castlight fades, creating a vivid silhouette on the horizon. | One of the rarest lives-on‑nature experiences in Africa. | | **Community of lions and elephants** | Garamba’s “big‑game” community includes savannah elephants, hippos, lions, and buffalos. | A full “safari range” experience, but with minimal tourist intrusion—you’ll likely see giraffes without ever leaving the roadside. | | **UNESCO heritage** | 4 902 km² of mosaic landscapes; the park’s huge buffer zone protects the wildlife and the local communities’ livelihoods. | Your presence indirectly supports the conservation programs that keep the giraffes alive. | --- ## Quick reference for planning | Item | Detail | Source | |------|--------|--------| | **UNESCO World Heritage ID** | 136 | [UNESCO World Heritage List page](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/136/) | | **Current Kordofan giraffe count** | ~92 (2024) | [Giraffe Conservation Foundation update](https://giraffeconservation.org/programs/kordofan-giraffe-conservation-in-drc/) | | **Peak viewing period** | Dry season Dec‑Mar; always travel with professional guides | [African Parks safety brief](https://www.africanparks.org/garambas-population-kordofan-giraffe-growing-heres-why) | --- ### Bottom line for you If you’re flying to the DRC in June 2025 and want to see a Kordofan giraffe, **Garamba National Park** is your single, viable choice. It’s a UNESCO World Heritage site that hosts the last remaining Kordofan giraffe population in the country, and the park is run by a professional conservation partnership (African Parks; The **Kordofan giraffe** (_**Giraffa antiquorum**_[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-:1-2) or _**Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum**_) is a species or subspecies of giraffe found in northern Cameroon, southern Chad, the Central African Republic, and possibly western Sudan.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-range-3) They usually live in tree savannas, bush savannas and thorn savannas.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-:0-4) Compared to most other subspecies, the Kordofan giraffe is relatively small at 3.8 to 4.7 m (12 ft 6 in to 15 ft 5 in),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-5) with more irregular spots on the inner legs. There are around 2,300 individuals living in the wild.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-6) In the wild, female Kordofan giraffes live in loose groups, whilst males live solitary.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-:0-4) They have an average lifespan of around 35 years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-:0-4)
_The Christian Science Monitor_ lists only 38 individuals being alive in the embattled Garamba National Park in The Democratic Republic of Congo due to poaching; their skin is used for luxury goods and they are said to produce enough meat to feed poachers for weeks._[citation needed_] Recent genetic studies also shows distinct genetic populations of giraffes that makes conservation of these subspecies even more important.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-7)

The population in the Bénoué Complex, Cameroon (a landscape that consists of three national parks: Bénoué National Park, Faro National Park, Bouba Njida National Park; interconnected by 29 hunting zones), numbers fewer than 300 individuals as of 2023.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-onlinelibrary.wiley.com-8) Illegal hunting represents the greatest threat to the subspecies, particularly in Bénoué National Park, where it may become locally extinct without further conservation interventions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-onlinelibrary.wiley.com-8)
The Kordofan giraffe eats a variety of sticks, leaves and bark, usually of Acacia trees. Additionally they eat grasses, buds, as well as seeds.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-Baselzoo-9) Like other giraffes, they classify as herbivores.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-:0-4)
Its English name is a reference to Kordofan in Sudan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-:1-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kordofan_giraffe#cite_note-range-3)

The **Kordofan giraffe** (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_) is a subspecies of giraffe. Its English name is a reference to Kordofan in Sudan.

## Appearance
Compared to most other subspecies, Kordofan giraffes are relatively small, with more irregular spots on the inner legs. A median lump is present in males.

### Geography

Kordofan giraffes are found in southern Chad, the Central African Republic, northern Cameroon, and the northeastern DR Congo. Their habitat includes savannas with shrubs and sparse trees, and open bushland.
Kordofan Giraffe

## Habits and Lifestyle
Little is known about the behavior of Kordofan giraffes. Generally, giraffes are found in groups that vary in size and composition. These groups are usually sex-segregated although mixed-sex groups made of adult females and young males also occur. Young males also form groups and engage in playfights. However, as they get older, males become more solitary but may also associate in pairs or with female groups. Like all giraffes, they are not territorial, but they have home ranges that vary according to rainfall and proximity to human settlements. Males occasionally roam far from areas that they normally frequent. Male giraffes use their necks as weapons in combat, a behavior known as "necking". Necking is used to establish dominance and males that win necking bouts have greater reproductive success. Giraffes browse during the first and last hours of the daytime. Between these hours, giraffes mostly stand and ruminate. Rumination is the dominant activity during the night when it is mostly done lying down.

## Diet and Nutrition
Giraffes are herbivores (folivores, lignivores, frugivores). They typically browse on leaves, fruits, twigs of trees, and flowers of woody plants, primarily acacia species.

Giraffes are polygynous, meaning that males mate with multiple females. ## Population
### Population threats
The primary causes of giraffe population declines are habitat loss and direct killing for bushmeat markets. These beautiful animals have been extirpated from much of their historic range, and now protected areas like national parks provide important habitat and anti-poaching protection to giraffe populations.

## Population
### Population number
According to IUCN Red List, the total population size of the Kordofan giraffe is around 1,942 individuals, of which around 1,400 are probably mature individuals. Currently, this species is classified as Critically Endangered (CR) on the IUCN Red List and its numbers today are decreasing.

## Population
### Ecological niche
Giraffes have a great effect on the trees that they feed on, delaying the growth of young trees for some years and giving "waistlines" to too tall trees. In addition, when spotting a predator, they can serve as a warning system for other nearby animals.

## Habits and Lifestyle
Little is known about the behavior of Kordofan giraffes. Generally, giraffes are found in groups that vary in size and composition. These groups are usually sex-segregated although mixed-sex groups made of adult females and young males also occur. Young males also form groups and engage in playfights. However, as they get older, males become more solitary but may also associate in pairs or with female groups. Like all giraffes, they are not territorial, but they have home ranges that vary according to rainfall and proximity to human settlements. Males occasionally roam far from areas that they normally frequent. Male giraffes use their necks as weapons in combat, a behavior known as "necking". Necking is used to establish dominance and males that win necking bouts have greater reproductive success. Giraffes browse during the first and last hours of the daytime. Between these hours, giraffes mostly stand and ruminate. Rumination is the dominant activity during the night when it is mostly done lying down.

### Population threats
The primary causes of giraffe population declines are habitat loss and direct killing for bushmeat markets. These beautiful animals have been extirpated from much of their historic range, and now protected areas like national parks provide important habitat and anti-poaching protection to giraffe populations.

According to IUCN Red List, the total population size of the Kordofan giraffe is around 1,942 individuals, of which around 1,400 are probably mature individuals. Currently, this species is classified as Critically Endangered (CR) on the IUCN Red List and its numbers today are decreasing.

# Kordofan Giraffe Conservation in DRC
Garamba National Park in DRC is the last haven for the Kordofan giraffe in the country. Despite threats from poaching and rebel activities, GCF, African Parks, and the DRC government have successfully achieved a steady increase in giraffe numbers.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Garamba National Park is home to the last remaining population of Kordofan giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_), a subspecies of the northern giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis_). Established in 1938 as one of Africa’s first national parks, Garamba stood out for its uniqueness. However, its reputation has been marred by the activities of rebel insurgents (Lord’s Resistance Army) resulting in the loss of the last northern white rhino.
Over the past few decades, poaching has decimated the park’s wildlife, as rebel groups often resort to selling wildlife products to fund their illegal activities. Recognizing the dire situation, the Giraffe Conservation Foundation has collaborated with African Parks and DRC’s wildlife authority, ICCN, since 2016 to save the last natural giraffe population in the country.
Our collaborative efforts have focused on gaining a deeper understanding of population dynamics, habitat use, and immediate threats. The team of African Parks, with the support of the Giraffe Conservation Foundation, implements conservation monitoring and management activities through regular aerial and vehicle-based surveys to monitor all individually-identified giraffe.
The targeted giraffe conservation efforts have resulted in Kordofan giraffe numbers in the park and surrounding areas gradually increasing to over 100 giraffe. This positive trend underscores the importance of continued support for this crucial giraffe conservation initiative, which is slowly transforming into a remarkable success story.

Garamba National Park in DRC is the last haven for the Kordofan giraffe in the country. Despite threats from poaching and rebel activities, GCF, African Parks, and the DRC government have successfully achieved a steady increase in giraffe numbers.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Garamba National Park is home to the last remaining population of Kordofan giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_), a subspecies of the northern giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis_). Established in 1938 as one of Africa’s first national parks, Garamba stood out for its uniqueness. However, its reputation has been marred by the activities of rebel insurgents (Lord’s Resistance Army) resulting in the loss of the last northern white rhino.
Over the past few decades, poaching has decimated the park’s wildlife, as rebel groups often resort to selling wildlife products to fund their illegal activities. Recognizing the dire situation, the Giraffe Conservation Foundation has collaborated with African Parks and DRC’s wildlife authority, ICCN, since 2016 to save the last natural giraffe population in the country.
Our collaborative efforts have focused on gaining a deeper understanding of population dynamics, habitat use, and immediate threats. The team of African Parks, with the support of the Giraffe Conservation Foundation, implements conservation monitoring and management activities through regular aerial and vehicle-based surveys to monitor all individually-identified giraffe.
The targeted giraffe conservation efforts have resulted in Kordofan giraffe numbers in the park and surrounding areas gradually increasing to over 100 giraffe. This positive trend underscores the importance of continued support for this crucial giraffe conservation initiative, which is slowly transforming into a remarkable success story.

## Kordofan Giraffes — Congo's Rarest Giants
The **Kordofan giraffe** (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_) is one of the most endangered giraffe subspecies in the world, with fewer than 2,000 individuals remaining in the wild. Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is one of its last strongholds.
Distinguished by their paler coloring and irregular patches that extend further down their legs compared to other subspecies, Kordofan giraffes were once widespread across Central and West Africa. Today, their range has collapsed dramatically.
African Parks, in partnership with ICCN (Congo's wildlife authority), has significantly improved the park's security and infrastructure since 2005, creating conditions for wildlife recovery and limited but growing tourism access.

## Where to See Kordofan Giraffes in DRC — Complete Safari Guide
Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is home to critically endangered Kordofan giraffes, forest elephants, hippos, and lions — one of Africa's oldest and most exclusive national parks, managed by African Parks with zero tourist crowds.

## Kordofan Giraffes — Congo's Rarest Giants
The **Kordofan giraffe** (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_) is one of the most endangered giraffe subspecies in the world, with fewer than 2,000 individuals remaining in the wild. Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is one of its last strongholds.
Distinguished by their paler coloring and irregular patches that extend further down their legs compared to other subspecies, Kordofan giraffes were once widespread across Central and West Africa. Today, their range has collapsed dramatically.
African Parks, in partnership with ICCN (Congo's wildlife authority), has significantly improved the park's security and infrastructure since 2005, creating conditions for wildlife recovery and limited but growing tourism access.

*   **Late Season (November):** Showers fade, roads dry out and crowds are still absent.
